forces: Soprano and accompaniment; acoustic scoring unestablished
intro: Scarpia demands Tosca’s body as the price of her lover’s freedom. Emmy Destinn sings the prayer in which Tosca, a singer herself, puts her life in art and love before God.

sections.label: A · Tosca accounts for her life
sections.mNote: Art, love and secret acts of charity

sections.label: B · Flowers, jewels and prayers
sections.mNote: The soprano recalls her gifts to the church

sections.label: C · The question returns
sections.mNote: Tosca asks God why he repays her with suffering

cues.title: A singer’s prayer
cues.text: “Vissi d’arte, vissi d’amore” — “I lived for art, I lived for love.” Tosca begins with the two things she has trusted. She insists that she has harmed nobody and has quietly helped people in need.
cues.evidence: Illica and Giacosa, Tosca (1900), Act II, Vissi d’arte; La Scala libretto, p. 34. https://www.teatroallascala.org/static/upload/tos/tosca-libretto-accessibile.pdf . Translation ours.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Scarpia waits for an answer
cues.text: Scarpia has had Cavaradossi tortured and condemned. Now he offers Tosca her lover’s life in return for sex. She tries to flee; he reminds her that he holds Mario. The prayer happens with her tormentor still in the room.
cues.evidence: Illica and Giacosa, Tosca (1900), Act II, the confrontation immediately before Vissi d’arte; La Scala libretto, pp. 30–34. https://www.teatroallascala.org/static/upload/tos/tosca-libretto-accessibile.pdf

cues.title: Flowers on the altar
cues.text: Tosca’s faith has taken ordinary, tangible forms: prayers, flowers on the altar, jewels for the Madonna’s mantle. She has also given her singing to the stars. The aria gathers these offerings before the words turn back towards her own pain.
cues.evidence: Illica and Giacosa, Tosca (1900), Act II: the central verses of Vissi d’arte name the prayers, flowers, jewels and singing. La Scala libretto, p. 34. https://www.teatroallascala.org/static/upload/tos/tosca-libretto-accessibile.pdf
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Destinn in the studio
cues.text: Emmy Destinn records this aria for Victor on 23 April 1914; the disc is Victor 88487. In December 1910 she had created Minnie in Puccini’s La fanciulla del West at the Metropolitan Opera, opposite Caruso and under Toscanini. Tim Ecker made the digital transfer, Adam Cuerden the slight restoration.
cues.evidence: The Commons description gives Victor 88487, matrix C-14508-4, the recording date of 23 April 1914, Tim Ecker’s digital transfer and Adam Cuerden’s slight restoration: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Emmy_Destinn,_Vissi_d%27arte_(Tosca).ogg . The Giacomo Puccini Catalogue of the Works lists the first performance of La fanciulla del West at the Metropolitan Opera on 10 December 1910, with Destinn as Minnie, Caruso as Johnson and Toscanini conducting: https://catalog.puccini.it/public/works/la-fanciulla-del-west

cues.title: The unanswered question
cues.text: “Perché me ne rimuneri così” — “Why do you repay me like this.” Tosca returns to the question with which she has already interrupted her prayer. When the aria ends, Scarpia answers with a command: “Risolvi!” — “Decide!”
cues.evidence: Illica and Giacosa, Tosca (1900), Act II: the final question of Vissi d’arte and Scarpia’s next line; La Scala libretto, p. 34. https://www.teatroallascala.org/static/upload/tos/tosca-libretto-accessibile.pdf . Translations ours; Scarpia’s reply belongs to the opera, beyond this solo recording.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: He could make a whole theatre wait with a woman at a window, then break its heart with a tune it had heard before.
facts: Lucca; Milan Conservatory, 1880–83, with Bazzini and Ponchielli
Giulio Ricordi · Luigi Illica and Giuseppe Giacosa · Giuseppe Adami and Renato Simoni
Twelve operas, counting Il trittico as three; a Mass, songs and chamber music
composer.background:
Puccini began at the organ. His family had supplied Lucca with church musicians for generations, and when his father Michele died in 1864, the five-year-old Giacomo was expected to continue the trade. He studied in the town, played in its churches and completed a Mass in 1880. But in 1876 he had heard Verdi’s Aida in Pisa. The theatre won. A scholarship helped him into the Milan Conservatory, where Antonio Bazzini and Amilcare Ponchielli taught him composition. His graduation piece of 1883, Capriccio sinfonico, contains the bustling music that would eventually open La bohème.

His first opera nearly went nowhere. He submitted Le Villi to the Sonzogno competition on the last possible day, 31 December 1883; it failed even to receive a mention. The librettist Ferdinando Fontana arranged a private hearing at the journalist Marco Sala’s house, with Arrigo Boito among the guests. A subscription paid for a performance at Milan’s Teatro Dal Verme the following May. Giulio Ricordi bought the opera and commissioned another. Edgar, first performed at La Scala in 1889, was a failure that Puccini spent years trying to repair.
